units.title: Validity, soundness, and the fallacies that actually persuade

lessons.title: Valid versus sound: the distinction, and how it is used to mislead
lessons.explanation: Lesson 79 introduced validity; this lesson separates validity from soundness and examines why the gap between them is the most exploited gap in ordinary argument. Validity is a property of an argument, not of a sentence: an argument is valid when it is impossible for its premises all to be true while its conclusion is false. The premises are supposed to guarantee the conclusion, so a valid argument is truth-preserving, not truth-establishing. Soundness adds a second, entirely different requirement: a sound argument is valid and has all true premises. Two consequences follow immediately. A valid argument with one false premise proves nothing about its conclusion, because it also licenses the conclusion's negation if you alter the false premise; validity transmits falsity as faithfully as it transmits truth. And a valid argument can be a bad argument: the inference from 'snow is white' to 'snow is white' is valid and tells you nothing you did not already accept. Aristotle's Prior Analytics is the historical origin of the systematic study of validity through the syllogistic, and the modern model-theoretic account states validity as the absence of any interpretation on which the premises hold and the conclusion fails. The misleading use is usually a compression: a speaker asserts a conclusion with confidence, offers a valid-looking inference, and leaves the controversial premise unstated. Aristotle called this an enthymeme, an argument with a suppressed premise, and its rhetorical advantage is that the burden of proof never touches the weakest link. So the practical rule for this lesson is procedural: before assessing an argument, make every premise explicit and file it as either a logical or a factual question.
lessons.example: A hiring committee argues: (1) if a candidate's teaching evaluations are above the departmental median, the candidate is an effective teacher; (2) this candidate's evaluations are above the median; (3) therefore this candidate is an effective teacher. The form is modus ponens and the argument is valid. Now check premise (1). It is an empirical generalisation claiming that evaluation scores are a sufficient indicator of teaching effectiveness, and it is contested: scores are known to correlate with grading leniency and with characteristics unrelated to learning. A single false premise makes the argument valid and unsound, so the conclusion is unestablished. Compare a second argument from the same file: (1) most effective teachers have above-median evaluations; (2) this candidate has above-median evaluations; (3) therefore this candidate is an effective teacher. Both premises may be true and the conclusion may be true, yet the argument is invalid: it affirms the consequent, since an above-median score is compatible with ineffectiveness. These two failures need different repairs. To repair the first you must investigate the world and defend or discard premise (1); to repair the second you must supply the missing inference, which would require the false premise that only effective teachers score above the median. Now watch the misleading compression. A dean announces that 'it has been proven that small classes improve outcomes'. Ask what was actually established. Suppose the underlying study measured an association between class size and attainment. The enthymeme runs: class size correlates with attainment, therefore reducing class size raises attainment. The suppressed premise is that the association is causal rather than confounded, and it is exactly the premise that carries the argument's practical force. Naming the suppressed premise converts an announcement into an assessable claim, and that is all this lesson asks you to do.
lessons.question: An argument has all true premises and a true conclusion yet is invalid. What, precisely, does that combination establish about the argument's conclusion?
lessons.answer: Nothing about the conclusion's truth or falsehood is established by the argument, because the truth of premises and conclusion here is coincidental rather than transmitted by the inference
lessons.distractor: It establishes that the argument is inductively strong rather than deductively valid, since true premises and a true conclusion cannot coexist with invalidity
lessons.correction: Validity is a property of the inference, and invalid arguments frequently have true premises and true conclusions; the pattern of a true conclusion resting on a non-sequitur is the standard case of an argument that cannot transmit support. The distractor invents a principle that true premises with a true conclusion rule out invalidity, which is false, and it substitutes induction for what may be a bad deductive inference.

depth.definitions: An argument is a set of propositions in which some, the premises, are offered as support for another, the conclusion. Validity: it is impossible for all premises to be true and the conclusion false; equivalently, no interpretation of the non-logical vocabulary makes the premises true and the conclusion false. Soundness: valid plus all premises true. Validity and soundness apply to arguments; truth and falsity apply to propositions; validity does not apply to a single sentence. An enthymeme is an argument with one or more premises suppressed. A counterexample interpretation is an assignment of meanings or values that makes the premises true and the conclusion false, which is how invalidity is demonstrated. Deductive consequence guarantees truth; inductive consequence makes the conclusion probable given the premises and is defeated by added premises, which deductive validity never is. Prerequisites: the notion of an argument form from lesson 79 and the idea of a premise as a claim with its own evidential status.
depth.mechanism: The distinction does real work because validity and soundness are answerable to different investigations with different kinds of evidence. Validity is settled by logic: you test form, look for a counterexample interpretation, or produce a derivation. Soundness requires empirical or conceptual work on each premise. That division is what the misleading compression exploits. When a speaker asserts a conclusion and gestures at an inference, an audience tends to evaluate the inference, which is often impeccable, and to leave the load-bearing premise unexamined. The model-theoretic account of consequence makes the logical question sharp: validity is the absence of a model of the premises that is not a model of the conclusion. Note three limits. First, the account is formal, so it captures consequence in virtue of form rather than entailment in virtue of meaning, and material or analytic entailments need separate treatment. Second, validity is not sufficient for a good argument: question-begging and premise-redundant arguments are valid, so additional norms (relevance, non-circularity, the epistemic status of the premises) are required. Third, in real discourse premises are typically incomplete, so assessing an argument requires charitable completion first, and a completion that strengthens the argument is a reconstruction you must flag rather than attribute.
depth.secondExample: The misleading can run the other way, against a sound argument. Consider a dispute about a warehouse fire. The argument runs: (1) if the sensor reading was accurate, no one was in the loading bay at nine; (2) two independent witnesses and a badge log place someone in the loading bay at nine; (3) therefore the sensor reading was not accurate. The form is modus tollens, hence valid, and each premise has ordinary evidential support, so the argument is plausibly sound. The company's lawyer replies that the sensor is a certified instrument with a long reliability record, so the reading stands. That reply has true premises about the sensor's general reliability, and its conclusion about the reading at nine does not follow, because the inference is invalid: the general reliability of an instrument does not settle whether this reading was accurate, and premise (2) is left untouched. The reply is an ignoratio elenchi, an argument that misses the point at issue while sounding responsive. The philosophical payoff is symmetrical to the first example: there, a valid inference hid a contested premise; here, a true general fact hides a non-sequitur, and an audience that checks only whether the lawyer's claim about the sensor is true will endorse an argument that never engaged the case for inaccuracy.
depth.mistake: Four misconceptions recur. The first conflates predicates: 'a valid truth' or 'a sound conclusion' treats validity and soundness as properties of propositions rather than of arguments. The second infers soundness from a true conclusion, which reverses the direction of support, since a true conclusion is compatible with an invalid argument and with false premises. The third infers that an invalid argument establishes the falsehood of a conclusion; instead, invalidity establishes only that this argument failed, and the conclusion may be supported by a different argument or may be true for reasons nobody has stated. The fourth treats a soundness verdict as available from logic alone. Diagnostics: ask which question the speaker is answering. If the reply concerns the reasoning, it bears on validity; if it concerns a premise, it bears on soundness. A speaker who responds to a challenge about a premise by improving the inference, or to a challenge about the inference by defending a premise, has changed the subject, and that shift is often the whole rhetorical manoeuvre.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Collect three arguments from sources you actually read this week: one from an opinion piece, one from a textbook or lecture, and one from an argument in which you were a participant. For each, do four things and write them down. First, render the premises explicitly, supplying any suppressed premise with the weakest plausible version rather than the most convenient one. Second, test validity by attempting to describe an interpretation on which every premise is true and the conclusion false. Third, label each premise supported, contested, or unsupported, naming the kind of evidence that would settle it. Fourth, state a verdict of the form valid and sound, valid and unsound, or invalid, and say what single change would repair the argument. Model response for the opinion piece: if the piece argues that a policy failed because outcomes worsened after its introduction, the explicit premises are that outcomes worsened and that the policy caused the worsening; the argument is valid only with the causal premise added; that premise is contested and would be settled by comparison with a counterfactual or a control group; the verdict is valid and unsound pending that evidence; the repair is either to supply the counterfactual or to weaken the conclusion to an association. Self-review rubric, four points: (1) no suppressed premise is left implicit in your rendering; (2) the validity test names the specific interpretation you tried, including the one you could not construct; (3) each premise's evidential status is labelled rather than asserted; (4) the repair you propose actually addresses the defect you identified, rather than a different one.
depth.summary: Validity and soundness answer different questions, and almost every ordinary case of persuasive bad reasoning is a compression that asks an audience to check one while the argument depends on the other. The transferable discipline has three moves: complete the argument, test the inference, then test the premises, and report which of the two tests failed. Applied to writing, it means stating your own suppressed premises rather than hoping they pass unexamined, because a premise you might have to defend in public is a premise you should defend before publishing. Applied to reading, it converts a disagreement about conclusions into a disagreement about a specific premise or inference, which is the only form of disagreement that can be settled.

visual.title: The two-gate test for an argument, with the compression that bypasses gate two
visual.description: A diagram of an argument flowing through two independent gates: form first, then the truth of each premise, with the enthymeme path shown bypassing the second gate.
steps: Argument arrives: explicit premises, an inference, and a conclusion
Gate one, validity: attempt a counterexample interpretation with all premises true and the conclusion false. Outcome: valid or invalid, a verdict about the inference only
Gate two, soundness: each premise is examined separately and labelled supported, contested, or unsupported, with the kind of evidence that would settle it named
Route A, valid and all premises supported: the argument is sound and the conclusion is established by it
Route B, valid but at least one premise contested: the argument is unsound, and the pending work is empirical or conceptual, not logical
Route C, invalid: the inference cannot transmit any support, whatever the premises turn out to be
The compression: the suppressed premise is never displayed, so an audience checks gate one, approves, and never arrives at gate two

lessons.title: The fallacies that are actually common, and the long lists that are not
lessons.explanation: Introductory courses teach a list of named fallacies, and the list itself has a history that is worth knowing. As the Stanford Encyclopedia entry on fallacies records, the standard textbook inventory descends from Irving Copi's Introduction to Logic of 1961, which presented eighteen informal fallacies, and these in turn spring from two sources: Aristotle's Sophistical Refutations and Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding. The entry's working definition is that a fallacy is an argument that seems to be better than it really is, and the seductive appearance is doing genuine work in that definition. Now the criticism. Following the earlier attack by Hamblin, Maurice Finocchiaro observed that introductory textbooks contain very few examples of actual fallacies and concluded that fallacies, understood as types of logically incorrect argument, are probably not common. That is a strong claim, but the weaker and better supported point is enough: a list assembled for pedagogy and inherited over centuries is not a frequency table. Once you separate the questions, three different things come apart. There are formal errors of inference that are genuinely common in ordinary reasoning, such as affirming the consequent, as in the hiring example of lesson 91. There are patterns of reasoning whose frequency has been studied empirically in the psychology of judgement, notably base-rate neglect and the conjunction error documented by Tversky and Kahneman, and the striking content-sensitivity of the Wason selection task, first reported in 1960, where most people fail an abstract version and many succeed when the same logical structure is clothed in a social rule. And there are items on the standard list whose frequency in real argumentation is largely doctrinal, such as the blanket ban on appeals to authority, which cannot be a general error because relying on experts is unavoidable, and which turns into a genuine error only when the cited authority lacks the relevant expertise, is speaking outside it, or has an interest that bears on the claim.
lessons.example: At a school board meeting a parent argues against a proposed increase in class sizes. She says two things. First, the district's own paid consultant reported that class size does not affect attainment. Second, her neighbour's daughter was in a class of forty and did well. A student trained on the standard list might label the second claim a fallacy of anecdotal evidence and the first an appeal to authority, and then stop. Both labels are doing less than they appear to. The anecdotal claim is not an argument at all; it is a single observation presented as if it were a sample, and its persuasive force comes from the salience of one vivid case, which is a documented feature of judgement rather than a defect in an inference. Nothing is refuted by noticing that it is one case; the work is done by asking what would count as evidence at the level of the whole district. The appeal-to-authority label is worse than unhelpful here, because the consultant may be exactly the relevant expert, and the SEP's discussion of authoritative testimony makes clear that the epistemically interesting difference is between a layperson who knows a little and a genuine epistemic authority, someone who is both an epistemic superior and an expert in the domain in question. The real questions about the consultant are narrower and answerable: is the domain the right one, does the report actually say what the parent claims, and does the consultant have an interest in the outcome? Finally, notice the task-sensitivity result in the Wason selection task. Performance on the same logical form changes dramatically with content, which means the error is not a fixed trait of the reasoner but a function of the problem's presentation. That is a fact about how to teach and how to design a decision, not a Latin name.
lessons.question: Finocchiaro argues that fallacies, understood as types of logically incorrect argument, are probably not common. What is the most defensible inference for a student of argument to draw from that claim?
lessons.answer: Separate the question of how often an error pattern occurs in real argument from the question of whether a named fallacy is available to apply, and test any frequency claim about a fallacy against evidence rather than against its presence on a teaching list
lessons.distractor: Treat the claim as settling that named fallacies do not exist as categories, so no argument should ever be assessed by asking whether it resembles a listed fallacy
lessons.correction: Finocchiaro's observation is about textbook examples and the tractability of the category of fallacy, and it displaces the pedagogical authority of the lists rather than abolishing the errors they name. Affirming the consequent remains an error whether or not it is frequent, so the correction is to stop inferring frequency from a list, not to stop reasoning about inference.

depth.definitions: A fallacy, in the standard treatment, is an argument that seems better than it really is, so the appearance condition is built into the definition: a transparently bad argument is not a fallacy in this sense. Formal fallacies are invalidities of form. Informal fallacies are errors that depend on content, context, or dialectical setting. Ignoratio elenchi is the argument that misses the point at issue, and the straw man is a variation in which the opponent's position is distorted to make it easier to refute. The fallacy fallacy is the invalid inference from the presence of a defective argument to the falsehood of its conclusion. Base-rate neglect is the failure to incorporate prior frequency information. The Wason selection task is a test of conditional reasoning whose difficulty depends sharply on the content of the rule. Prerequisite: the validity and soundness vocabulary of lesson 91; this lesson adds the question of how errors are classified and how often they occur.
depth.mechanism: The appearance condition earns its place because it explains why reasonable people err and because it draws a line between careless slips, which need attention, and seductive reasoning, which needs training. The SEP entry notes an alternative demarcation that does not use appearance at all, namely frequency: fallacies are the mistakes we must learn to guard against because they recur noticeably. That alternative makes the question empirical, and this is where the long lists fail. A list organised for teaching optimises for coverage of historically named patterns, and the stock examples are chosen to illustrate the pattern rather than to sample real discourse. Two further mechanisms explain why name-first teaching backfires. First, a rich vocabulary of labels invites identification over diagnosis, so a reader who spots a resemblance to a named pattern feels the argument has been dealt with. Second, the labels are thick with context: an appeal to authority is fallacious only relative to a domain and a question, and an ad hominem is sometimes exactly on target when the issue at hand is the speaker's credibility. Both effects are amplified by a dialectical setting that rewards point-scoring, which is a failure mode that the argumentation literature discusses directly rather than as a fallacy.
depth.secondExample: Contrast two cases to see when labelling earns its keep. Case one: a council member proposes congestion charging for the city centre. A respondent tells the meeting that the member wants to ban all cars and put drivers out of work. That is a straw man, more precisely a variation of ignoratio elenchi in which the position is substituted, and the SEP's example of the move makes both errors visible: the proponent does not hold the attributed position, and even if the attributed position were false that would not make the original proposal false. Here the label earns its keep because it identifies the exact step that failed, which is the substitution, and it tells you what to ask for, which is the actual proposal. Case two: a reader dismisses a climate scientist's finding as an argument from authority. Here the label blocks inquiry. The scientist may be the relevant expert, the finding may be supported by independent evidence elsewhere, and the speaker's status as an expert is a reason to give the claim weight rather than a reason to discount it. The diagnostic that separates the cases is whether naming the pattern locates a defective inferential step. If it does, you have a criticism; if it merely terminates attention, you have a slogan.
depth.mistake: Four misconceptions are worth correcting explicitly. The first is that every bad persuasive argument has a Latin name; many failures are omissions of evidence, framing effects, or failures to define the question, none of which is an argument-form error. The second is the fallacy fallacy: showing that a defence of a conclusion is defective does not show the conclusion is false, since a different defence may succeed. The third is that ad hominem is always illegitimate; when credibility is the question at issue, such as whether a witness is telling the truth about a transaction, the speaker's character is directly relevant. The fourth is that memorising a longer list produces better reasoning. Diagnostics: ask whether the named pattern is present in the explicit premisory structure rather than in the tone; ask whether the fault concerns the inference or a premise; and ask what a good version of this argument would look like, because that question restores the burden of proof to the right place.
depth.application: Non-blocking task, one week. Keep a fallacy log of exactly three arguments you encounter: one from a news source, one from an argument made to you, and one from an argument you made. For each, write four short entries. First, the argument in explicit premise-conclusion form. Second, the step that actually failed, described in your own words and without a Latin name. Third, whether a standard name applies, and if so whether applying it locates the defective step or merely labels the argument. Fourth, an honest frequency judgement: is this a pattern you have met often, and what evidence beyond this instance supports that judgement. Model response for the news source: a piece infers that a benefit change caused a decline in claims because claims fell after the change; the defective step is the inference from sequence to cause; the name post hoc ergo propter hoc applies and does locate the step; the frequency judgement is that this pattern is very common in reporting and the evidence for that judgement is the count in your own log rather than a textbook. Self-review rubric, four points: (1) every entry names a step, not a mood; (2) at least one entry concludes that no standard label was needed; (3) the frequency judgement cites your own observations rather than a list; (4) the entry about your own argument identifies a real defect rather than an incidental one.
depth.summary: Named fallacies are a historical inheritance assembled for teaching, and their value is diagnostic rather than predictive: they help you name a failed step once you have found it, and they mislead when used to classify an argument before the step has been found. The transferable skill is a division of labour between three questions: what is the defective step, does an established name apply to it, and how often does this pattern actually occur. Only the first question is about this argument; the second is vocabulary; the third is an empirical question that requires evidence, and the honest answer is usually that we know less than the labels suggest.

visual.title: Three questions about an error pattern, kept separate
visual.description: A diagram in which a single argument is routed through three independent questions: what failed, does a name apply, and how common is the pattern, with evidence requirements shown at the third.
steps: Question one, diagnosis: state the argument explicitly and identify the step that failed, in plain words, without using a fallacy name
Question two, classification: check whether an established name applies, and record whether applying it locates the failed step or merely labels the argument
Question three, frequency: estimate how often the pattern occurs, and name the evidence for that estimate, such as a count in your own log, a corpus study, or an admission that you have none
Warning path one: classifying before diagnosing, which produces labels that terminate inquiry
Warning path two: inferring a conclusion's falsehood from a defective defence of it, which is the fallacy fallacy
Warning path three: treating a list of names as a frequency claim, which mistakes a teaching inventory for data

lessons.title: Thought experiments: what they can and cannot establish
lessons.explanation: A thought experiment is an imagined scenario used to test a claim, to generate one, or to make a theory's commitments visible. The Stanford Encyclopedia's taxonomy shows that the interesting disagreement is not about whether thought experiments are used, since they are ubiquitous, but about what they can establish. The most sceptical position in the literature is Pierre Duhem's, whose 1913 discussion is usually read as an outright condemnation: a thought experiment, he claimed, is no substitute for a real experiment and should be forbidden in science and in science education. That reading is now contested, and the Encyclopedia notes that Buzzoni has questioned it, arguing that Mach's reception of Duhem already indicates a more nuanced view. It also notes that the usual defence of scientific thought experiments, namely that they can at least be checked by physical experiment, is simply false, because a frictionless plane or a universe empty of material bodies cannot be produced in any laboratory, and philosophical thought experiments cannot be even approximately tested. Within this dispute three accounts matter most for you. John Norton's argument view holds that any thought experiment is really an argument, possibly disguised, beginning from premises grounded in experience and proceeding by deductive or inductive rules, so that the picturesque features are psychologically helpful and strictly redundant. James Robert Brown's intuition-based account, in its Platonic version, holds that a few special cases deliver a priori knowledge of nature, fallible but not derived from data; his paradigm is Galileo's falling-bodies experiment, where attaching a light musket ball to a heavy cannon ball generates a contradiction in the Aristotelian account and thereby shows that all bodies fall at the same rate. Thomas Kuhn's conceptual constructivism holds that a good thought experiment creates an anomaly in a ruling theory and helps practitioners reconceptualise the world, contributing to paradigm change. Ernst Mach's experimentalism treats thought experimenting as a limiting case of experimenting, resting on an experience in thought.
lessons.example: Work through Galileo's case, because it shows the difference between a robust negative result and a contested positive one. The Aristotelian theory says heavy bodies fall faster than light ones. Take a heavy cannon ball H and a light musket ball L. On the theory, H falls faster than L. Now fasten them together. The compound object H+L is heavier than H, so on the theory it must fall faster than H. But the compound includes the light ball, which drags, so on the theory it must fall more slowly than H. The theory yields both H+L is faster than H and H is faster than H+L. That is a contradiction, and the result is genuinely negative and robust: no new measurement was required, and the inference is a reductio of a stated commitment. Brown's further claim is stronger and contested, namely that the episode delivers a priori knowledge that all bodies fall at the same speed. Here the reconstruction matters. If you accept the argument view, the thought experiment is a set of empirical premises about weight, drag, and composition plus a reductio, and its yield is the removal of a theory rather than the positive establishment of a new law. Brown's reply is that no new data entered and the conclusion was not derived from old data, which is why he classifies it as a priori. The Encyclopedia records a technical challenge to the claim that the result is a logical truth. So the honest verdict for this lesson is layered: the thought experiment robustly refutes the Aristotelian claim, it does not by itself settle the equally fast claim without further assumptions about drag and composition, and which of those you emphasise depends on which account of thought experiments you accept.
lessons.question: Galileo's falling-bodies argument is treated in the literature as a paradigm thought experiment. What is the most defensible description of what a single well-constructed reductio of this kind establishes?
lessons.answer: It establishes that a stated theory is internally inconsistent or that a proposed analysis fails, which is a negative, conceptual result, and it does not by itself establish any new empirical regularity
lessons.distractor: It establishes the true account of the phenomenon directly, because no new data are involved and the conclusion therefore cannot be contaminated by observational error
lessons.correction: The absence of new data cuts both ways: it is what makes the result conceptual, and it is also why the positive conclusion needs premises about drag, composition, and idealisation that the scenario alone does not supply. The distractor converts the thought experiment's freedom from measurement error into a positive empirical warrant, which is exactly the inference Brown's critics refuse.

depth.definitions: A thought experiment is a hypothetical scenario constructed and evaluated in thought, in order to test, motivate, or refute a claim. A reductio ad absurdum is an argument showing that a set of commitments entails a contradiction, so at least one commitment must be given up. The argument view holds that a thought experiment is a disguised argument from empirical premises. An intuition-based account holds that some thought experiments deliver a priori knowledge of nature by way of intuition, and comes in naturalistic and Platonic versions. Conceptual constructivism holds that thought experiments work by making a theory's concepts reorganise, so they create anomalies and can drive paradigm change. Experimentalism, associated with Mach, treats thought experimenting as a limiting case of real experimenting, resting on a Gedankenerfahrung, an experience in thought, that draws on past experience of the world. Inquiry resistance, introduced properly in lesson 97, is the mark that distinguishes a conceptual boundary from a gap in information. Prerequisites: validity and soundness from lesson 91, and counterexample reasoning from lesson 80.
depth.mechanism: A thought experiment works by exploiting conceptual and theoretical connections that an audience already accepts, which is why its force varies with the audience's commitments. Reconstructed as an argument, the premises are the described scenario, the theoretical claims about the entities in it, and a bridge principle such as the assumption that a proposed analysis must be answerable to considered judgement. The conclusion then follows by the rules of the inference, and the picturesque narration contributes to persuasion rather than to validity. That reconstruction is attractive to empiricists and is defended by Norton, but the Encyclopedia records that it faces objections, the first being that the notion of argument invoked is too vague to do the work asked of it. The alternative accounts locate the philosophical work elsewhere: in intuition, in conceptual reorganisation, or in tacit, experience-based know-how. The limits that matter for evaluating real cases are these. First, a thought experiment's premises include idealisations, so its result holds of the idealised scenario and carries over to the world only by an additional argument. Second, judgements about scenarios are not uniform, and their variation with wording and order is an empirical finding that any argument relying on a shared intuition must reckon with. Third, a scenario's imaginability does not entail its possibility, so an argument from conceivability to possibility needs a bridge principle of its own. Fourth, a thought experiment that cannot in principle be checked by any further consideration is doing something other than testing a hypothesis, and the Encyclopedia's remark that philosophical thought experiments cannot even be approximately tested is a caution rather than a refutation, because a reductio does not require testing.
depth.secondExample: Contrast two further uses. Use one is a thought experiment as an analysis-breaker, which is the mode with the clearest epistemic credentials. A proposed definition of knowledge as justified true belief is refuted by describing a case in which the subject has a justified true belief but lacks knowledge, and the refutation works if the case is coherent and the description is accurate: the analysis entails a prediction about the case, and the case falsifies the analysis. This is the structure sketched in lesson 71 and it requires no new empirical investigation, which is why it is robust. Use two is a thought experiment as a heuristic for a positive theoretical claim. Einstein's clock in the box and elevator scenarios functioned as devices for clarifying what a theory of gravity must explain and for generating arguments rather than as self-contained proofs: the physical theory still had to be developed and checked against observation. The contrast is instructive because it shows the difference between a thought experiment that closes a question by producing an inconsistency and one that opens a question by making a structure visible. When you meet a thought experiment, ask which role it is playing, and evaluate it against the standard for that role.
depth.mistake: Four misreadings recur. The first treats a thought experiment as evidence of an empirical fact, which mistakes an idealised scenario for a data point. The second assumes that because a scenario is imaginable its conclusion follows, ignoring the bridge principle from conceivability to possibility. The third treats a famous and oft-cited thought experiment as settled, when the Encyclopedia shows disputes about paradigmatic cases are live and the standing of a canonical example is not itself an argument. The fourth, and most common in seminar discussion, thinks that if intuitions about a scenario are not universal the thought experiment is worthless. That is too quick in both directions: a reductio needs only the specific commitments that generate the contradiction, not unanimous intuition, while a positive claim resting on a contested intuition needs to explain why competent readers differ, which is often more productive than either asserting or dismissing the result.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Choose a thought experiment you have met in a text you are actually reading, not one recalled from a summary, and reconstruct it twice. In the first reconstruction, present it as an explicit argument in Norton's style: numbered premises including the idealisations and the bridge principle, an inference whose validity you check, and a stated conclusion. In the second, state what the least defensible premise is, and whether the thought experiment could survive its removal. Then write three sentences classifying the case as a reductio of an analysis, a positive theoretical claim, or a heuristic device, and say which account of thought experiments your reconstruction presupposes. Model response for a personal-identity fission case: the premises are that a subject divides into two continuers, that whatever relation preserves identity must be one-one, and that both continuers are equally related to the original; the inference is a reductio of the identity criterion; the least defensible premise is the one-one requirement, since it encodes a substantive commitment rather than an observation; the case is an analysis-breaker rather than a positive claim. Self-review rubric, four points: (1) idealisations are stated as premises rather than hidden; (2) the bridge principle is explicit; (3) the classification is defended against the alternative classifications; (4) the account of thought experiments you rely on is named.
depth.summary: Thought experiments are powerful at showing that a set of commitments is inconsistent and weak at establishing new empirical claims, because their yield depends on idealised premises and on bridge principles that the scenario itself does not supply. The transferable skill is to reconstruct any thought experiment as an argument, mark its idealisations, and ask what the argument would be worth if the least secure premise were removed. This applies directly to the puzzles you meet in ethics and metaphysics, where a vivid case is often doing the work of an argument, and to the empirical sciences, where an imaginary scenario can clarify a question without deciding it.

visual.title: A thought experiment decomposed into an assessable argument
visual.description: A diagram separating the narrative surface of a thought experiment from the argument underneath, with the idealised premises and bridge principle shown as separate components that carry the epistemic burden.
steps: Surface layer: a vivid scenario told in prose, which recruits intuition and supplies no premises by itself
Premise layer one, described scenario: what the case states, including every idealisation such as frictionless planes or perfect duplication
Premise layer two, background theory: the accepted claims about composition, causation, or analysis that the case relies on
Bridge layer: the principle licensing the move from the scenario to the claim, for example that an analysis must answer to considered judgement, or that conceivability implies possibility
Inference layer: the rule by which the conclusion follows, typically a reductio when the result is negative and an ampliative step when it is positive
Verdict layer: negative results that isolate an inconsistency are robust; positive results inherit the weakness of the bridge layer and the idealisations
Objection markers: the notion of argument may be too vague, intuitions vary with presentation, and the scenario may be imaginable without being possible

lessons.title: Other minds: what inference from behaviour can and cannot reach
lessons.explanation: Lesson 76 asked what the mind is; this lesson asks how you could know that anything else has one. The Stanford Encyclopedia's entry observes that the traditional epistemological problem was preoccupied in the mid-twentieth century less with a general doubt about minds than with solipsism, the question whether I am alone in the universe, and it accepts that certainty is unavailable while asking whether good reason is nonetheless available. Three families of response are set out. The argument from analogy is the traditional one, and the entry states its canonical form in the writing of John Stuart Mill, who asks by what evidence he knows that the walking and speaking figures he sees and hears have sensations and thoughts, and answers by citing the similarities between their bodies and his own. Analogical reasoning cites similarities and concludes that further similarities may be taken to exist, so the thought is that other bodies resemble mine and their behaviour resembles my behaviour when I have a given experience, therefore they have experiences when they behave like that. The argument from best explanation, defended as an advance by Pargetter, holds that positing minds is rational because it is the best available explanation of the behaviour, and the entry notes that David Chalmers treats it as about as good a solution to the problem of other minds as we are likely to get, while Hyslop insists that any justification must still make crucial reference to one's own case. The third family is the criteria view associated with Wittgenstein, who contrasts citing a criterion of a mental state with offering a symptom of it, and who warns against the misleading parallel of treating psychology as if it studied private processes the way physics studies physical ones. Beyond the epistemological problem lies the conceptual one, which asks not whether I can know about other minds but how I acquired the concept of a mind at all when the only mind I have been given is my own. The naturalist turn reframes the question again, through theory-theory and simulation theory.
lessons.example: A clinician assesses whether a patient who cannot speak is in pain. The observations available are behaviour and physiology: guarding of the abdomen when the bed is moved, a facial grimace, withdrawal on palpation, an elevated heart rate, and a change in these responses after an analgesic is given. Run the three accounts over the same evidence. Under the argument from analogy, the clinician reasons that when he himself is in pain he guards and grimaces, and this patient is guarding and grimacing, so this patient is probably in pain. Notice the weakness precisely: the analogical base is one case, his own, and the inference needs a further premise, that similar behaviour has similar causes, which is the very claim under dispute. The inference is not worthless, but it is a very thin inductive base and it is vulnerable to the objection that it reasons from a single instance. Under the argument from best explanation, the claim that the patient is in pain is justified because it explains the whole pattern, including the response to analgesia, which would be a coincidence on the alternative hypothesis that nothing is felt. This is the shape of inference by which unobservable entities earn their place in the sciences, and its cost is that it must specify what makes one explanation better than another, since simplicity and scope are themselves contested currencies. Under a criteria account, the clinician does not infer at all: the grimace under these circumstances is a criterion of pain, not a symptom of it, which is to say that it partly constitutes what it is evidence for, and the concept of pain is grasped through such public expressions rather than through a private inner sample. The three accounts diverge most sharply in a case with minimal behaviour, where criteria accounts lose their grip and the explanatory account still has physiology and the response to intervention to work with.
lessons.question: The argument from analogy for other minds is often criticised for resting on a single case. What does that criticism identify, and what does it leave standing?
lessons.answer: It identifies that the analogical base is one instance, one's own case, and that the inference needs an unargued uniformity premise; it leaves standing the possibility that the belief is justified by the best explanation of behaviour rather than by analogy
lessons.distractor: It identifies that analogy is never a legitimate form of reasoning about minds, which refutes all behavioural evidence of other minds and leaves only the criteria view standing
lessons.correction: The single-case objection is a complaint about the inductive strength of one specific argument, not a verdict on analogy as such, and the entry on analogy and analogical reasoning sets out the criteria by which analogical arguments are evaluated, including relevance and the strength of the shared features. Nothing in the objection rules out behavioural evidence; it rules out treating the analogy form as the only available justification.

depth.definitions: The epistemological problem of other minds is the problem of justifying belief that others have mental states. Solipsism is the doctrine that only one's own mind exists. The argument from analogy reasons from similarities between oneself and others to further similarities, here to the presence of mental states. The argument from best explanation, often called inference to the best explanation, holds that a hypothesis is justified when it is the best available explanation of the evidence. A criterion of a mental state, in Wittgenstein's sense, is something whose presence in the appropriate circumstances is a ground for attributing the state, as contrasted with a symptom, which is a reliable but defeasible correlate discovered by experience. The conceptual problem of other minds is the problem of how the concept of a mind acquires content given that one's acquaintance with minds begins with one's own. Theory-theory holds that we attribute mental states by deploying an implicit folk-psychological theory; simulation theory holds that we use our own mind as a model and run it off-line. Prerequisites: the mind-body options of lesson 76, and the explanation-and-understanding material that lesson 99 develops further.
depth.mechanism: The structural reason that inference from behaviour is underdetermined is that behaviour is public while, on the Cartesian picture inherited from lesson 76, mental states are private, so any inference crosses a boundary that no observation crosses with it. The analogy argument has a further defect beyond the size of its base: the uniformity premise it needs, that like behaviour has like causes, cannot be established by more of the same reasoning without circularity, since the only case in which behaviour and experience are jointly observed is one's own. Best-explanation arguments avoid the circularity by appealing to explanatory virtues, but they inherit the difficulty of specifying those virtues in a way that is not merely a description of what we already believe, and they must meet the objection that positing other minds is not a hypothesis we can independently test, since the evidence for it and the practice of attribution are entangled. Criteria accounts dissolve the inference rather than repair it, holding that the privacy premise is what generates the problem and should be rejected, so that seeing the grimace is seeing the pain. Their cost is that they sit uncomfortably with cases where expression and state come apart, which is precisely why the naturalist programmes matter empirically: developmental work on children's belief-desire psychology, and work on the mechanisms by which we track others, treat the question as one about the capacities that produce attribution rather than about a private inference.
depth.secondExample: Consider a system that produces fluent, context-appropriate reports about its own internal states: it says it is uncertain, reports a preference, and revises its reports when new information arrives. The same three accounts return different verdicts. Best-explanation reasoning says the attribution of states is warranted insofar as the hypothesis explains the pattern of outputs and predicts future ones, and it is indifferent in principle to the substrate. A criteria account must ask whether the relevant circumstances make the report a criterion rather than a symptom, and here the distinction bites, since a report produced by a mechanism designed to produce reports may be a symptom without being a criterion. The conceptual problem then presses hardest: what would it mean for the attribution to be true or false if we have stipulated the mechanism? The comparative value of the case is that it isolates a disagreement about what the dispute is even about. Similar pressure arises with animals: the inference from behaviour to suffering is uncontroversial for many species and contested for others, yet the practical stakes, in how they are treated, can be higher than in the human cases that preoccupy the literature, so the choice of evidential threshold has moral consequences rather than only epistemic ones.
depth.mistake: Four errors are common. The first states the problem as whether others behave as I do, which is not in doubt for most cases, whereas the problem concerns their having experiences at all. The second concludes that because mental states are unobservable they are unknowable, which confuses unobservability with inaccessibility and ignores the standing of explanatory inference in the sciences generally. The third reads Wittgenstein's criteria view as behaviourism, the doctrine that mental talk is talk about behaviour, when the point is about the grammar of attribution rather than about the elimination of the mental. The fourth treats theory-theory and simulation theory as a purely philosophical dispute to be settled by intuition, when both make predictions that developmental and neuropsychological evidence bears on, and when the fusion of the two positions is itself a live option. Diagnostic question: which of the mental states at issue could be attributed on behavioural grounds alone, and for which does the argument need something more, such as the response to intervention or the testimony of the person?
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Choose a case where the attribution of a mental state to a being is genuinely contested and where your answer would change how someone is treated: an animal, a patient with a disorder of consciousness, an infant, or a software system. Write an assessment with four parts. First, list the evidence actually available, separating behaviour, physiological measures, and reports. Second, state what the argument from analogy would conclude and what its uniformity premise would be. Third, state what the best-explanation argument would conclude, and name the explanatory virtue that does the work, such as scope or the ability to predict the response to an intervention. Fourth, state what a criteria account would say, and identify any case in which the criteria and the explanatory verdict diverge. Finish with two sentences naming the evidential threshold you would adopt and what makes the alternative threshold unattractive. Model response for an animal case: behaviour and physiology give the evidence; analogy concludes from similarity of nociception and withdrawal; best explanation concludes from the fit of the pain hypothesis with the response to analgesia and with the avoidance learning curve; criteria accounts say the distress behaviour in these circumstances is expressive rather than merely symptomatic; the thresholds differ for fish and for insects, and the reason to adopt the lower threshold is asymmetry of error, since a false negative permits avoidable suffering. Self-review rubric, four points: (1) the evidence is separated by kind rather than pooled; (2) the uniformity premise is stated in words; (3) the explanatory virtue named is one the case actually exercises; (4) the threshold you adopt is defended against the cost of the error it invites.
depth.summary: The problem of other minds is not whether other people behave as you do but whether anything is felt behind that behaviour, and the arguments for other minds are vulnerable in different places: analogy to the thinness of a one-case inductive base and to a circular uniformity premise, best explanation to the specification of explanatory virtue, and criteria accounts to cases where expression and state come apart. The transferable skill is to state which account of attribution you are relying on and what evidence would change your verdict, because the same discipline governs how you treat animals, patients, infants, and machines, and there the stakes are practical rather than academic.

lessons.title: Testimony and trust: is believing what you are told rational by default?
lessons.explanation: Almost everything you believe about the world arrived through other people: the date of a treaty, the safety of a drug, the contents of the building you are in. Lesson 87 examined epistemic injustice in credibility assignment; this lesson takes the prior question of whether testimony is a source of justification at all, and on what terms. The Stanford Encyclopedia sets out the debate as a disagreement over a requirement called Positive Reasons. Reductionists hold that a hearer is justified in believing what a speaker says only if the hearer has positive reasons for thinking the speaker's testimony reliable, where those reasons are not themselves ultimately based on testimony, and has no undefeated defeater indicating the testimony is false or unlikely. The view traces back at least to Hume, and modern versions are associated with Elizabeth Fricker, Adler, Lyons, Lipton and others. Its central motivation is gullibility: if we could accept testimony without positive reasons, the reductivist asks, what would stop us accepting anything? Non-reductionists deny Positive Reasons and endorse a Presumptive Right: a hearer is justified in believing what a speaker says provided she has no undefeated defeater indicating that the testimony is false or unlikely, with some versions adding that she must be counterfactually sensitive to defeaters in her environment. The view traces to Thomas Reid and has been defended by Austin, Coady, Burge, Plantinga, Williamson and others. Beyond this dispute the entry distinguishes knowledge transmission from knowledge generation, noting cases in which a hearer knows on the basis of testimony even though the speaker does not know, which blurs a sharp transmission account; it distinguishes evidential from non-evidential views of how testimony justifies; it contrasts individualism with anti-individualism about our epistemic dependence on others; and it examines authoritative testimony, where a preemptive account holds that an epistemic authority's word should replace one's own reasoning on the matter, and a non-preemptive account treats expert testimony as one more item of evidence to be integrated.
lessons.example: Work three versions of one exchange. A patient is told by a nurse that her new medication must be taken with food. The reductionist asks what positive non-testimonial reasons the patient has for the nurse's reliability on this point. She can consult the printed leaflet, ask the pharmacist, and check whether the instruction matches what was said at the appointment. Notice what happens when she pursues this: the leaflet was written by someone she has not met, the pharmacist relies on training she cannot verify, and the appointment note was made by a clinician. Each check is itself mediated by testimony, so the reductionist demand, applied to every link, threatens a regress in which almost nothing survives, including most of the science the patient would need in order to evaluate the claim at all. The non-reductionist says she needs no positive reasons, only the absence of a defeater, and the interesting cases are precisely the defeaters: if she learns the nurse confused her with another patient, the presumption is defeated and belief is no longer justified. Now the authoritative version. Suppose the instruction comes from a pharmacist with a specialist qualification in this drug class, so he is both an epistemic superior and an expert in the relevant domain. A preemptive account says the patient should not reopen the question using her own partial reasoning, since that is exactly what expertise is for; a non-preemptive account says she should treat his advice as strong but fallible evidence and weigh it with the rest. The two accounts diverge visibly if she has read a plausible blog post contradicting him. The practical stakes appear when an institution says that people must simply trust its guidance. Whether that is an appropriate demand depends on whether the source is genuinely an epistemic authority in the relevant domain and whether its preemption is justified, which are the questions the literature on authoritative testimony actually addresses.
lessons.question: A reductionist about testimony requires positive non-testimonial reasons for trusting a speaker. What is the strongest difficulty that this requirement faces?
lessons.answer: Applied consistently, it threatens to undermine most of what we know, because our checks on most speakers are themselves mediated by other people's testimony
lessons.distractor: It cannot explain why a hearer who lacks any undefeated defeater should nonetheless sometimes withhold belief, since the presence of a defeater is the only relevant variable
lessons.correction: The objection from the ubiquity of testimony is the standard pressure that motivates non-reductionism and hybrid views, because the reductionist's reasons must be obtainable without reliance on testimony for the view to avoid circularity. The distractor describes the non-reductionist position, not a difficulty for the reductionist, and conflates the two views.

depth.definitions: Testimony, in the epistemological sense, is the transmission of a propositional content by a speaker to a hearer, in a context that does not require the hearer to do independent investigation. Reductionism about testimony: justification for believing a speaker requires positive reasons for the speaker's reliability, not themselves based on testimony, plus the absence of undefeated defeaters. Non-reductionism: a presumptive right to believe, defeated only by an undefeated defeater. A defeater is a consideration indicating the belief is false or unlikely or is based on an unreliable process; a rebutting defeater counts against the content, an undermining defeater against the grounds. An epistemic authority is a person who is both an epistemic superior and an expert in the relevant domain. Preemptive accounts of authoritative testimony hold that the authority's claim should replace one's own reasoning; non-preemptive accounts treat it as strong evidence to be weighed. Prerequisites: the justification material of lesson 72 and the credibility discussion of lesson 87; this lesson adds the norm governing a source you cannot check.
depth.mechanism: The disagreement turns on what a presumption is and how much it carries. The reductionist's argument is a slippery-slope argument: if no positive reasons are required, then there is no epistemic difference between believing a careful informant and believing a random stranger, and gullibility becomes rational. The non-reductionist replies that the presumption is defeasible and that the social and institutional environment supplies the missing discrimination, since hearers are typically alert to defeaters and their alertness is itself a background condition of trust. A third position, hybrid, distinguishes minimal and substantial independence: a hearer must have some monitoring capacity without requiring positive reasons for each speaker. The literature also separates evidential from non-evidential views of how testimony justifies belief, and individualist from anti-individualist pictures of epistemic dependence, where anti-individualism holds that a hearer can know on the basis of a speaker's competent epistemic work even if she could not have carried it out herself. That anti-individualist picture is what makes a division of epistemic labour defensible, and it is why the reductionist demand is so costly: it asks every hearer to reproduce the epistemic work that the division of labour exists to avoid. The account of authoritative testimony shows how the same distinctions generate different advice, since preemption and non-preemption recommend opposite responses to an expert who contradicts your own reading.
depth.secondExample: Take scientific knowledge, where the structure of the problem is starkest. Almost no one can reproduce a clinical trial, verify a particle detection, or check a carbon-dating result, yet the claims are believed and acted on. Under a strict reductionist requirement, this widespread belief looks unjustified, which many take to be a reductio of the requirement rather than of the belief. Under non-reductionism, the beliefs are justified by default, and the work shifts to identifying defeaters, which is where the interesting cases live: a researcher with a direct financial interest in the outcome, a finding published once and not replicated, an institution whose incentives reward a particular result, or a body of evidence known to be selectively reported. Each of these is a genuine defeater, and a non-reductionist who treats the presence of a defeater as irrelevant to belief has simply misunderstood her position. The contrast with the patient case is illuminating: there, the checkable leaflet grounded a modest positive reason and the defeater was a specific error of identification, while here the defeater is structural and concerns the source's incentives rather than any particular claim.
depth.mistake: Four misconceptions recur. The first says that trusting testimony is irrational, which presupposes reductionism and ignores the regress argument against it. The second says that non-reductionism licenses believing whatever one is told, which misses defeasibility: the view changes the default, not the ceiling. The third says that consulting an expert settles the matter, which assumes preemption while the preemptive and non-preemptive accounts are rivals, and which also assumes the source is an epistemic authority when that is precisely what must be checked. The fourth treats the debate as a historical quarrel between Hume and Reid with no live content, when the entry's material on authoritative testimony, group testimony, and anti-individualism shows it is being actively developed, and when the practical version of the question, how much trust an institution may ask for, is a live public issue. Diagnostic: identify whether the disagreement concerns the default (presumption versus positive reasons) or the trigger for retreat from the default (which defeaters count).
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Choose one belief you hold that rests entirely on testimony you cannot check: a medical instruction, a legal rule, a historical claim, or a factual claim about a place you have never visited. Write four short paragraphs. First, state the belief and identify the immediate source and the chain behind it as far as you can trace. Second, run the reductionist test and record what positive non-testimonial reasons you actually possess, noting each point at which a proposed check turns out to rely on further testimony. Third, run the non-reductionist test and list every defeater you can identify, ordering them as undermining or rebutting. Fourth, state your verdict on whether belief is justified, and state whether you would treat the source as an epistemic authority and, if so, whether on a preemptive or a non-preemptive basis. Model response for a medication instruction: the source is a pharmacist, the chain runs through the licence, the training, and the manufacturer's data; reductionist checks such as the leaflet and a second opinion each turn out to be testimony-borne; the defeaters are whether the pharmacist asked about interactions and whether the manufacturer has a sales interest, the second being undermining rather than rebutting; the verdict is that belief is justified, and the pharmacist counts as an epistemic authority in this domain, so a preemptive account is defensible for the narrow question of interactions while it would not be for a question about the patient's own preferences. Self-review rubric, four points: (1) the chain is traced rather than assumed; (2) at least one proposed check is acknowledged to be testimony-borne; (3) defeaters are classified rather than listed; (4) the authority judgement states the domain in which authority is claimed.
depth.summary: Testimony is a genuine source of justification whose norm is contested: reductionism demands positive non-testimonial reasons and risks a regress, non-reductionism grants a defeasible presumption and must say which defeaters defeat it. The transferable skill is to separate three questions whenever you rely on someone's word: what is the default, what would defeat it, and is the source an epistemic authority in the domain at issue. That structure governs how you read expert guidance, how you respond when an institution asks for trust, and how you judge your own credulity without collapsing into either gullibility or blanket suspicion.

visual.description: A decision diagram showing what a hearer is entitled to assume, what removes the entitlement, and whether the source holds domain-specific authority requiring preemption or integration.
