questions.prompt: A committee rejects a proposal with the reasoning: 'If the pilot programme had worked, participation would have risen, and participation rose, so the pilot worked.' A second member objects that the conclusion does not follow. Which assessment is correct, and what does it tell you about the argument's premises?
questions.answer: The inference is invalid because it affirms the consequent, and the premises may all be true and even the conclusion true while the argument transmits no support
questions.distractor: The inference is valid, so the argument is sound if participation did in fact rise and would in fact have risen had the pilot worked
questions.correction: Rising participation is compatible with many causes other than the pilot, so the pattern of inference cannot guarantee the conclusion. The distractor treats a necessary condition as a sufficient one and then adds the mistaken step of treating soundness as a matter of the premises being true, when validity must be established independently.

questions.prompt: A reader responds to a newspaper column on housing supply by saying that the author's claim is undermined by the fact that he owns several rental properties. Assess this response using the level's treatment of fallacies and of credibility.
questions.answer: Whether the response is a fallacy depends on what is at issue: if the question is the author's credibility or the presence of a conflict of interest, the fact is directly relevant, whereas if it is offered as a reason the claim is false it substitutes an attack for an argument
questions.distractor: The response is an ad hominem attack and is therefore fallacious regardless of the subject under discussion, since a speaker's circumstances never bear on the truth of a claim
questions.correction: Ad hominem is a defect only when irrelevant, and the SEP treatment makes relevance the discriminating feature rather than the presence of the attack. The distractor's absolute rule is itself the error, because interests and expertise often bear on how much weight a claim should receive.

questions.prompt: An author defends a view of distributive obligation by describing a hypothetical society in which no one can plausibly claim to have earned their talents. A critic replies that the scenario is impossible. Evaluate the exchange.
questions.answer: The reply engages a premise the argument need not rely on, since the thought experiment can function as a reductio of a claim about entitlement or a device for making a commitment visible rather than as an assertion that the scenario occurs
questions.distractor: The reply is decisive, because describing an impossible scenario cannot yield any conclusion about obligations in the actual world
questions.correction: The robustness of a thought experiment turns on its role. As a reductio or an analysis-breaker it needs only an internally consistent scenario and a shared commitment, not the possibility of the case; as a positive empirical claim it would need the bridge principle the critic is implicitly demanding. The distractor applies the standard for the second role to the first.

questions.prompt: A researcher argues that a species of insect feels pain because its behaviour resembles the behaviour of vertebrates known to feel pain, and because blocking a specific neural pathway abolishes the behaviour. Identify what each strand of the argument is doing and where the weaker strand lies.
questions.answer: The resemblance claim is an argument from analogy with a thin comparative basis, while the intervention result supports the explanatory inference that pain best accounts for the behaviour and its abolition, so the intervention strand carries more weight
questions.distractor: Both strands are forms of the argument from analogy, so each depends on the single case of human experience and they stand or fall together
questions.correction: The intervention result does not reason from one's own case; it reasons that a hypothesis explains a pattern including the response to a manipulation, which is the best-explanation structure. Treating the two strands as one argument obscures why the researcher included the intervention at all. The distractor collapses a distinct inferential form into analogy.

questions.prompt: A patient is advised by a specialist to change treatment immediately, and she has read an article suggesting the opposite. She wonders whether she may take the specialist's word over her own reading. What does the level's material on testimony identify as the crux?
questions.answer: Whether the specialist is an epistemic authority in the relevant domain and whether authority preempts the patient's own reasoning or merely enters it as strong evidence
questions.distractor: Whether the patient has positive non-testimonial reasons for thinking the specialist reliable, since without such reasons belief is unjustified
questions.correction: The reductionist requirement is one contested position, and applied rigorously it runs into the regress problem, since the patient's own reading is itself testimony-borne. The crux is the preemption question plus the domain-specificity of the authority, which the distractor bypasses by presupposing one side of the default dispute.

units.title: Evidence, borderline cases, and reconstructing an argument fairly

lessons.title: The ethics of belief: when is evidence owed, and to whom?
lessons.explanation: Lesson 95 asked whether belief on testimony is rational by default. This lesson asks a different question: whether believing can be wrong, and if so in what sense. The founding exchange is between William Kingdon Clifford and William James. Clifford's 1877 essay opens with a case. A shipowner, about to send an emigrant ship to sea, knows the vessel is old and has needed repairs, and has doubts about her seaworthiness. He talks himself out of the doubts, satisfies himself that the ship is sound, and lets her sail. Clifford's point is not that the ship sank; it is that the shipowner would have been guilty even had it floated, because the wrong was in acquiring a belief on insufficient evidence. His summary line is uncompromising: it is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence. James's 1896 reply begins by conceding a great deal and then distinguishing cases. He defines a genuine option as one that is forced, living, and momentous: forced because the choice between the hypotheses cannot be avoided, living because both hypotheses are real possibilities for the chooser, momentous because the choice is significant and irreversible. His thesis is that our passional nature not only lawfully may but must decide an option between propositions whenever it is a genuine option that cannot by its nature be decided on intellectual grounds, and he adds that to say 'do not decide, but leave the question open' is itself a passional decision. The Stanford Encyclopedia organises the resulting terrain by distinguishing kinds of doxastic norm, prudential, moral, and epistemic, and by distinguishing strict from moderate evidentialism, where moderate evidentialism allows non-epistemic considerations to bear on what counts as sufficient evidence. It also distinguishes practical non-evidentialism, which is where James's argument is usually placed, from the epistemic variety that would claim belief without evidence can be epistemically justified.
lessons.example: Take a hiring case. A manager hears from a colleague that a candidate is untrustworthy about money, and without checking, forms the settled belief that the candidate is dishonest, and rejects the application on that basis. Examine it in two passes. Clifford's pass: the belief was acquired on insufficient evidence, and on his view the wrong was already done in the acquiring, independently of the outcome, so the fact that the candidate might in any case have been dishonest is irrelevant to the verdict on the manager. Notice that the manager did have an inquiry available, which matters, because the wrong is often best located in a failure of inquiry, something within his control, rather than in an act of belief-formation that may not be voluntary at all. James's pass: is this a genuine option? The manager's choice is not forced in the relevant sense, since he could suspend judgement and ask; the hypothesis that the candidate is dishonest may not be living for him, since hearsay in this setting is not a live hypothesis without corroboration; and while the decision is significant, the significance does not make the question undecidable on intellectual grounds. So the exception does not apply, and the case falls outside James's licence. Now a case that does apply. Someone must decide whether to marry, or whether to trust a friend after an ambiguous betrayal, where deliberation cannot settle the matter on the evidence available and the choice cannot be postponed without making a decision by default. James's argument is that the passional element is doing legitimate work here. Whether that establishes an epistemic justification or only a prudential one is a separate and contested question, and the Encyclopedia's distinction between practical and epistemic non-evidentialism is the instrument for keeping those apart.
lessons.question: Clifford argues that the shipowner would have been guilty even if the ship had safely reached port. What does that claim commit him to about the nature of the wrong involved?
lessons.answer: The wrong lies in forming the belief without adequate inquiry and evidence, so it is independent of the harm that happens to result and would be a wrong even in an outcome where no one is injured
lessons.distractor: The wrong lies in the negligent risk-taking that endangered passengers, so his guilt depends on the ship having been a real danger rather than on the state of his belief
lessons.correction: Clifford's counterfactual is precisely designed to detach the verdict from the harm, which is why the case is about the ethics of belief rather than about negligence. The distractor relocates the wrong to the risk imposed on others, which is a different and also defensible charge but is not what Clifford's stipulation establishes.

depth.definitions: A doxastic norm is a standard governing belief. Evidentialism is the view that belief is justified by fit with the evidence. Strict evidentialism holds that only epistemic considerations bear on justification; moderate evidentialism allows non-epistemic considerations, including moral ones, to affect whether a belief is proper. Practical non-evidentialism holds that where a question cannot be settled on intellectual grounds and the stakes require action, a belief may be justified on practical grounds; epistemic non-evidentialism makes the stronger claim that such a belief can be epistemically justified. A genuine option, in James's sense, is forced, living, and momentous. Doxastic involuntarism is the thesis that belief is not under direct voluntary control, which constrains how an ought governing belief can be read. Prerequisites: the justification material of lesson 72 and the responsibility discussion of lesson 83; this lesson adds the normative question of which standard governs a belief and who may demand compliance with it.
depth.mechanism: Two mechanisms drive the whole debate. The first is the availability of inquiry. If belief is not directly voluntary, then an ethics of belief must govern what is within one's control, which is attention, the search for evidence, and the weight given to it. Clifford's shipowner is a study in a failure of inquiry, and that is why his verdict survives the counterfactual outcome: he had the means to check and chose not to. The second mechanism is the plurality of norms. A single belief can be epistemically permitted and morally objectionable, for example when it concerns another person's character and is formed cheaply, and the SEP's separation of prudential, moral, and epistemic norms is what allows that combination to be stated without contradiction. Moderate evidentialism handles the same phenomenon differently, by letting the moral context shape what counts as sufficient evidence, so that a higher standard applies where the stakes concern a person's standing. The debate also has a social mechanism that lesson 87 supplies: which beliefs are treated as requiring evidence, and whose testimony is credited without it, is unevenly distributed, so an evidential standard enforced selectively becomes an instrument of injustice rather than a norm of inquiry. The limits of the literature are worth stating: the epistemic status of James's exception remains contested, the conditions for a genuine option are vague at the margins, and the question of whether beliefs can wrong people is a recent and unsettled research area.
depth.secondExample: Reverse the direction of the case. A person receives overwhelming evidence that her business partner has been misappropriating funds, and she refuses to believe it, not because the evidence is weak but because the belief is unbearable. Is this a failure in the same sense as the manager's? Clifford's framework suggests that refusing to believe what the evidence establishes is a failure, but the mechanism is different: the manager failed to inquire, whereas she has inquired and resists the conclusion, so the failure is one of proportion rather than of diligence, and it may be partly outside voluntary control, which is why the primary remedy is a change in what she attends to and how she records what she already knows. Now consider the opposite error, which is accepting a painful belief on thin evidence because it fits a self-image or a prejudice, the pattern lesson 92 associated with motivated irrationality. Putting the two together shows why the ethics of belief cannot be reduced to an injunction to believe less; it is a demand for proportion between evidence and the strength of the belief, together with a demand for the inquiry that the stakes make reasonable.
depth.mistake: Four misreadings recur. The first is that Clifford demands proof for every belief, which is impossible; his standard is sufficiency relative to the question, and he is explicit that the wrong is believing what the evidence does not support, not holding beliefs at all. The second is that James licenses believing whatever one prefers. He bounds his licence to genuine options that cannot be settled on intellectual grounds, and he says in the essay that in addressing an audience whose weakness is letting belief follow recklessly on a lively conception he would not preach the liberty of believing. The third is that the wrongness of a belief always depends on resulting harm, which Clifford's shipowner example is expressly constructed to deny. The fourth is that the question can be handled by asking whether the belief is true, which conflates the ethics of forming a belief with its accuracy, and which cannot guide inquiry because the truth is usually what one does not yet know. Diagnostic: ask which norm is in play, who has standing to demand compliance, and whether the repair required is more evidence or a different distribution of attention.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Choose a belief you formed in the past year about a person, and one you formed about a public matter. For each, write a structured audit with five entries. First, state the belief and its current strength. Second, state the evidence you actually had at the time of forming it, distinguishing what you observed from what you were told. Third, identify whether there was an inquiry you could have made and did not, which is where Clifford's mechanism usually applies. Fourth, run James's test: state whether the option was forced, living, and momentous, and whether it could in principle have been settled on intellectual grounds. Fifth, state which norm governs the belief, epistemic, moral, or prudential, and what the correction would be. Model response for a belief about a colleague's competence: the evidence at the time was one poor meeting and a remark from a third party; the available inquiry was to check the record of past work; the option was neither forced nor momentous, and the question was decidable on evidence, so James's exception does not apply; the governing norm is epistemic with a moral overlay, since the belief concerns a person's standing and was formed cheaply; the correction is to suspend and inquire rather than to hold the belief at full strength. Self-review rubric, five points: (1) observed evidence is separated from reported evidence; (2) at least one missed inquiry is named rather than implied; (3) all three of James's conditions are assessed, not just one; (4) the norm identified is the one actually governing the case; (5) the correction is proportionate rather than a blanket demand for more evidence.
depth.summary: The question is not whether beliefs may be held without proof but which standard governs a given belief, what lies within one's control, and who may demand compliance. Clifford locates the wrong in believing on insufficient evidence and detaches it from harm; James carves out a bounded exception for forced, living, and momentous options that cannot be settled intellectually, and the status of that exception is contested. The transferable skill is to separate the epistemic question from the moral and prudential ones, identify the inquiry the stakes made reasonable, and treat the standards you apply to others with the same rigour you apply to yourself, since selective evidentialism is the failure mode lesson 87 documented.

visual.title: A belief routed through three norms and one bounded exception
visual.description: A diagram showing how a belief is assessed against epistemic, moral, and prudential standards, with James's genuine-option test shown as the only gate that can license proceeding without intellectual settlement.
steps: Candidate belief about to be formed or revised, with the evidence actually available at that moment
Gate one, inquiry: was there a checking procedure within reach that was not used, which is where Clifford's mechanism locates the wrong
Gate two, proportion: does the strength of the belief match the weight of the evidence, on the moderate evidentialist reading of sufficiency
Gate three, norm kind: the same belief is tested as an epistemic matter, a moral matter concerning how it affects others, and a prudential matter concerning its consequences for the believer
Bounded exception: the genuine-option test, requiring the option to be forced, living, and momentous and to be undecidable on intellectual grounds
If the exception applies, practical considerations may legitimately decide, and whether that also yields epistemic justification is a separate contested question
Failure markers: believing against the evidence, believing on evidence that should have been sought, and refusing a belief the evidence establishes

lessons.title: Vagueness, borderline cases, and the sorites paradox
lessons.explanation: The Stanford Encyclopedia sets out three conditions that must be met for an argument to be an instance of the sorites paradox. First, a sorites series must be constructible for the predicate: a finitely ordered sequence of values on a dimension decisive of the predicate's application, such as a sequence of heights for the predicate 'tall'. Second, neighbouring values must differ only incrementally, either indiscriminably or slightly, and this incremental difference is supposed to guarantee that if the predicate applies to one member of a pair it applies equally to the other; following Wright, this property of a vague term is called its tolerance. Third, the predicate must be true of the first value in the series and false of the last. With those conditions met, the paradox follows by repeated modus ponens: one grain does not make a heap; if n grains do not make a heap then n+1 do not; therefore ten thousand grains do not make a heap. Each step is licensed by tolerance, the inference is valid, the endpoints are stipulated, and the conclusion is absurd, so something among the plausible components must be rejected. The responses divide according to which component is denied. Epistemicists, whose lineage the entry traces from Chrysippus through Cargile and Sorensen to Williamson, hold that vagueness is a form of ignorance: vague terms have sharp boundaries whose locations are hidden from us, so heaps are sharply divided from non-heaps and one of the conditional premises is simply false, and bivalence is preserved. Williamson's own account grounds the boundaries in the fact that meaning supervenes on use. Semantic approaches hold instead that vagueness is a feature of meaning, that borderline cases are neither determinately applicable nor determinately inapplicable, and that classical logic or semantics must therefore be revised, whether by degrees of truth, by supervaluationism, by subvaluationism, or by contextualism. The entry also records a response that embraces the paradox rather than resolving it, and connections with the liar paradox.
lessons.example: Take a triage rule that says patients with severe pain are treated first, applied on a scale of reported severity from zero to ten. The rule must be applied tonight, so the institution cannot leave the predicate undefined. Set up the sorites. A score of ten is severe. If a score of n is severe, then a score of n minus one is severe, since one point on a self-report scale is an incremental difference and cannot plausibly change whether the term applies. A score of zero is not severe. By repeated application, a score of six is not severe, and a score of seven is not severe, and so on to the bottom of the scale. The chain is valid and each link is plausible, yet the conclusion collapses the rule entirely. Now run the four responses over the same case, and watch the practical consequences diverge. The epistemicist says there is a fact of the matter: some score is the last severe one, and the institution is merely ignorant of where it lies. That preserves classical reasoning and bivalence, and it is uncomfortable in a context where the rule's application must be defensible to a patient, since the institution cannot say which score it is or how it would know. The supervaluationist says the sentence 'a score of six is severe' is neither true nor false, that each admissible sharpening of the term yields a verdict and the verdicts differ, so borderline cases are truth-value gaps and the rule needs a conventional tie-break rather than a discovery. The degree theorist says severity comes in degrees of truth and the threshold is a decision about where to place the cut. The contextualist says the extension shifts with the comparison class and the purposes at hand, so a score is severe relative to a ward full of minor injuries and not severe relative to a ward full of fractures. Notice that the second and fourth responses both preserve the sense in which the case is genuinely borderline, while the first denies it, and that this disagreement is about the metaphysics of meaning, not about the patient.
lessons.question: A hospital administrator says that with a fine enough measurement scale the vagueness of 'severe pain' would disappear, since more precise measurement would reveal the true boundary. Which response to the sorites does this claim presuppose, and what does it miss?
lessons.answer: It presupposes epistemicism, on which a sharp boundary exists and is hidden, and it misses that vagueness in the linguistic sense is resistant to inquiry, so a finer scale measures a different and stipulated predicate rather than discovering the boundary of the original one
lessons.distractor: It presupposes semantic indeterminacy, since on that view more precise measurement would remove the borderline region by making the predicate determinate
lessons.correction: Epistemicism is the view that the boundary exists and is unknown, which is exactly what the administrator's claim requires; semantic indeterminacy denies that there is a fact of the matter to be discovered, so it cannot underwrite the claim. The distractor reverses the two positions, and the substantive point is the inquiry-resistance of vagueness, which no improvement in measurement removes.

depth.definitions: A predicate is vague if it admits borderline cases, that is, cases in which competent speakers cannot settle whether it applies and in which further investigation does not settle it either. A sorites series is a finite ordered sequence of values on a dimension decisive of the predicate. Tolerance is the property that a vague term applies across incremental differences on that dimension. The sorites paradox is the derivation of an absurd conclusion from tolerance, the clear endpoints, and valid reasoning. Epistemicism treats vagueness as ignorance of a sharp boundary, preserving bivalence and classical logic. Supervaluationism treats a borderline case as a truth-value gap and evaluates sentences under all admissible sharpenings, counting a sentence true on all of them as super-true. Subvaluationism is its dual, counting a sentence true on some admissible sharpening. Degree theories assign intermediate truth values. Contextualism holds that the extension varies with context and purpose. Higher-order vagueness is the phenomenon that the boundary of a borderline region is itself vague. Prerequisites: the truth and belief distinctions of lesson 71 and the analysis-and-counterexample method of lesson 80.
depth.mechanism: The engine of the paradox is that tolerance, classical logic, and the clear endpoints cannot all hold together, so each solution denies one of them, and the disagreements among solutions concern which denial is least costly elsewhere. Epistemicism keeps classical logic and bivalence and pays with a sharp boundary that speakers cannot locate or discover, which sits awkwardly with the fact that ordinary speakers' judgements are not merely uncertain but genuinely unsettled in the way the entry marks by the notion of inquiry resistance. Supervaluationism and degree theories give up bivalence for borderline cases and must then explain how reasoning with truth-value gaps or degrees works, and how borderline cases can be described at all. Contextualism gives up the idea that the predicate has a context-free extension and must explain how the term maintains semantic unity across contexts. Every semantic solution then faces higher-order vagueness: if there is a boundary between severe and not severe, there is presumably a boundary between definitely severe and borderline, and the argument reapplies. The entry also notes a unification with the liar paradox, which is a sign that the difficulty is not an artefact of this predicate, and it draws broader lessons about meaning as use, about the truth schema, and about referential indeterminacy. Understanding those limits is what distinguishes a competent use of the paradox from a slogan about everything being relative.
depth.secondExample: Contrast a term whose vagueness is practically inert with one where it does institutional work, and add a term that looks vague but is not. 'Bald' is vague and the boundary is indifferent to any decision anyone must make. 'Death', in the sense used to determine when treatment may be withdrawn, is vague at its edges and consequential. But a third case is diagnostic in a different way: 'light' as applied to a suitcase and to a room is not vague at all; it is ambiguous, since the two uses have distinct meanings, and the tests differ. The SEP's comparison of vagueness with ambiguity and with generality is what supplies the test. A vague term admits borderline cases and resists inquiry; an ambiguous term has two or more meanings that can be separated by paraphrase and by translation; a general term applies to a wide range without any borderline difficulty. Misdiagnosing ambiguity as vagueness produces the conclusion that a term cannot be defined and therefore cannot be applied, when in fact the correct response is to separate the senses and define each. This is a common error when the term is normative, such as 'reasonable', which is both general and vague, and where separating its senses from its borderline cases is the first step in making a policy defensible.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first treats vagueness as mere imprecision and concludes that sharper measurement or stipulative definition solves the problem; a stipulative definition replaces the original predicate rather than sharpening it, which changes what is being decided. The second assumes that a hidden boundary must exist, which is epistemicism, a contested position rather than a default, and which imports its own costs. The third treats the paradox as a trick and so misses that it is a genuine inconsistency within a set of principles that are each independently plausible. The fourth, common when the term is normative, dismisses the whole issue by saying that everything is a matter of degree, which is either degree theory, in which case it needs a semantics for degrees, or nothing at all. Diagnostic: identify which of the three conditions for a sorites series you would deny, and check whether your denial also resolves the higher-order version of the argument.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Choose a term used in a rule you actually have to apply: 'severe', 'safe', 'reasonable', 'near', 'affordable', or 'consenting'. Write four parts. First, verify that the three sorites conditions are met by constructing the series and stating the decisive dimension, the incremental step, and the two endpoints. Second, write the argument in the modus ponens chain and state the absurd conclusion. Third, run each response over the case in three sentences: epistemicist, semantic indeterminacy, and contextualist, stating what each verdict means for what you should do tomorrow. Fourth, state which response you would adopt for the practical decision and what it costs you, and check whether the higher-order version of the argument reappears for your chosen response. Model response for 'near' in a rule about notification of a hazard: the dimension is distance, the increment is one metre, and the endpoints are one metre as near and one thousand metres as not near; the chain concludes nothing is near; the epistemicist answers that a boundary exists but cannot be located, which is useless for a notification rule and would need a convention anyway; the supervaluationist answers that a borderline case is neither in nor out, so the rule must specify a convention for the penumbra; the contextualist answers that nearness depends on the purpose of the notice and the audience's exposure, which suggests defining the rule by purpose rather than by distance; the cost of the supervaluationist route is that the convention is a stipulation the institution must defend as fair, and higher-order vagueness reappears at the edge of the convention, which is why institutions usually draw bright lines deliberately. Self-review rubric, five points: (1) all three sorites conditions are checked explicitly; (2) the decisive dimension and increment are named, not assumed; (3) the four responses yield distinguishable practical consequences; (4) the cost of the chosen response is stated; (5) the higher-order check is attempted rather than asserted to be solved.
depth.summary: Sorites reasoning shows that tolerance, classical logic, and clear endpoints cannot all be kept, so every response buys consistency somewhere and pays somewhere else. The transferable skill is to distinguish a genuinely vague term from an ambiguous or merely general one, to state which of the three conditions you would deny, and to notice that a decision context forces an institution to convert a vague predicate into a convention and then defend that convention as a choice rather than as a discovery. That last move is where the philosophy of vagueness meets law, medicine, and public administration.

visual.title: The sorites chain and the four places to cut it
visual.description: A diagram of a sorites series from clear application to clear non-application, with the tolerance link marked and four points at which a response may deny a component.
steps: Series constructed on the decisive dimension: one grain to ten thousand grains, zero metres to one thousand metres, a pain score of zero to ten
Condition one satisfied: the ordering is finite and lies on a dimension decisive of the predicate
Condition two, tolerance: neighbouring values differ only incrementally, so if the predicate applies to one it applies to the other
Condition three, endpoints: the predicate clearly applies at the first value and clearly fails at the last
Chain: repeated modus ponens runs from the first value to the absurd conclusion that the predicate never applies
Cut one, epistemicist: deny that we know where the boundary lies, keeping sharp boundaries and bivalence
Cut two, semantic: deny bivalence at the boundary, so borderline cases are truth-value gaps, degrees, or context-relative
Cut three, tolerance denied: treat the incremental premise as false at some point, which must then be identified and defended
Residual problem, higher-order vagueness: the boundary of the borderline region is itself borderline, so the argument re-forms one level up

lessons.title: Causation and correlation: what a probabilistic association can and cannot license
lessons.explanation: 'Correlation is not causation' is true as a warning and thin as a technique. The philosophical work is in saying what the missing ingredient is. Begin with Hume. Section seven of the first Enquiry examines the idea of necessary connexion, and Hume's regularity account holds that what we observe in the world is constant conjunction rather than any observed tie between events, so the necessity we attribute to causes comes from the mind's transition rather than from an impression of power. Causal claims therefore require a justification that observation alone does not supply. The modern probabilistic theory attempts to supply it with a probability-raising condition: the first formulation is that C raises the probability of E just in case the probability of E given C exceeds the unconditional probability of E, and the second, equivalent formulation, which the Stanford Encyclopedia adopts for consistency, is that the probability of E given C exceeds the probability of E given the absence of C. Reichenbach, Suppes and Cartwright used one formulation and Skyrms and Eells the other. The entry then shows why the condition is neither sufficient nor necessary. It is not sufficient because of the common cause: Reichenbach's Common Cause Principle states that if two events are positively correlated and neither is a cause of the other, there is a common cause of both that screens them off from each other, forming what he called a conjunctive fork, so the correlation is explained by a shared upstream cause rather than by either event acting on the other. It is not necessary because of background context and Simpson's paradox, where probability raising can reverse when the population is stratified. The entry's own illustration uses smoking, country residence, and lung cancer. The remedy, on the interventionist and causal-modelling side of the same entry, is to model the system as a graph and to ask what happens under an intervention, together with assumptions such as the Markov condition and faithfulness that make the structure identifiable from data.
lessons.example: Work the arithmetic of Simpson's paradox, because the reversal is easier to believe once you have computed it. The entry's illustration has smoking causing lung cancer while a stronger cause, urban pollution, works the other way, and smoking is much more common among rural residents. Build a population of twenty thousand in two strata, each of ten thousand people. In the rural stratum, two thousand are non-smokers with a cancer rate of five per cent, giving one hundred cases, and eight thousand are smokers with a rate of ten per cent, giving eight hundred cases, so the stratum rate is nine hundred in ten thousand, or nine per cent. In the urban stratum, eight thousand are non-smokers with a rate of thirty per cent, giving two thousand four hundred cases, and two thousand are smokers with a rate of thirty-five per cent, giving seven hundred cases, so the stratum rate is thirty-one per cent. Within each stratum smoking raises the cancer rate: ten per cent against five per cent in the rural group, and thirty-five per cent against thirty per cent in the urban group. Now pool the population and ignore residence. There are ten thousand non-smokers with two thousand five hundred cases in all, a rate of twenty-five per cent, and ten thousand smokers with one thousand five hundred cases in all, a rate of fifteen per cent. The aggregate therefore reports that smoking is associated with a ten percentage point reduction in cancer, while within every stratum it is associated with an increase. Both summaries are arithmetically correct; they answer different questions, and the aggregate one is answering the question nobody asked. The argumentative lesson is exact: a claim of the form 'smoking does not cause cancer because smokers have less cancer' has a true premise and a conclusion that does not follow, and the missing element is a claim about what would happen under intervention on smoking while holding the background fixed.
lessons.question: Reichenbach's Common Cause Principle says that when two events are correlated and neither causes the other, a common cause screens them off from each other. What does that principle do to the probability-raising account of causation?
lessons.answer: It shows that probability raising is not sufficient for causation, because the correlation may be produced by a shared upstream cause rather than by the relation between the two events
lessons.distractor: It shows that probability raising is not necessary for causation, because a common cause can raise the probability of an effect without any correlation being present
lessons.correction: The common cause case is a counterexample to sufficiency: the inequality holds while the causal relation is absent, since the association is entirely accounted for by the shared cause. Insufficiency from confounders is a separate failure, illustrated by Simpson's paradox, where the inequality reverses or disappears under stratification. The distractor swaps the two failure modes and describes a case that would not even be a correlation.

depth.definitions: A regularity theory of causation holds that causation consists in constant conjunction plus the appropriate temporal and counterfactual features, with the felt necessity contributed by the observer rather than observed, on Hume's account. Probability raising is the condition that the probability of the effect given the cause exceeds the probability of the effect given its absence. Screening off occurs when conditioning on a third variable makes two variables probabilistically independent. A common cause principle states that correlations not explained by one variable causing the other are explained by a shared cause. A conjunctive fork is the structure in which a common cause screens off its two correlated effects. Simpson's paradox is the reversal or disappearance of an association when a population is partitioned by a background variable. An intervention is a manipulation of a variable that does not depend on its causes, and interventionist accounts treat causal claims as claims about the effects of interventions. Prerequisites: the probabilistic reasoning of the validity material in lesson 91 and the explanation material of lesson 99, which this lesson sets up.
depth.mechanism: The probabilistic account is attractive because it replaces an unobservable tie with an observable inequality, and it fails for two structurally different reasons. The first is confounding: an upstream variable that influences both terms generates an association without either causing the other, and no amount of data on the two variables alone reveals it, which is why the identification of causal structure requires either an intervention, a natural experiment, or a set of assumptions connecting the graph to the distribution. The second is that the inequality is not invariant under conditioning on a variable that lies between cause and effect, or on a variable that is a common effect of both, since conditioning on a collider can create an association where none exists in the population. Simpson's paradox is the public face of the first problem, and it is not a paradox at all once you see that the aggregate and the stratified associations are answers to different questions: the aggregate asks what the rate is among everyone who happens to smoke, while the intervention asks what the rate would be if smoking were assigned. The modelling apparatus sharpens the question by making the assumptions explicit, through the Markov condition, which links the graph to the probability distribution, and through minimality and faithfulness, which rule out gratuitous edges. Their limits are that they are idealisations, that many systems are too complex for reliable identification, and that mechanistic evidence may be required when no intervention is available.
depth.secondExample: Take a case where the association is the best evidence anyone will obtain. Suppose the question is whether a childhood condition affects an outcome decades later. Randomisation is not available and not ethical, so the evidence is observational. The discipline then has three legitimate routes. The first is to look for a natural experiment, some feature of the world that assigns exposure approximately independently of the outcome, such as a change in policy that affected one region and not another for reasons unrelated to the outcome. The second is to make the causal claim conditional and explicit about the assumptions it needs, stating which confounders are assumed absent and what would refute the claim. The third is to gather mechanistic evidence, connecting the exposure to the outcome through a pathway, which is the subject of lesson 99. Each route has a cost: natural experiments require the assignment to be plausibly independent, conditional claims are hard to act on, and mechanistic evidence is usually weaker than a well-identified effect. Contrast this with the smoking case, where cessation studies and dose-response gradients supply exactly the convergent evidence that the observational association alone does not. The comparison shows that the slogan is not a prohibition: associations can support causal conclusions, provided the argument supplies what the association by itself lacks.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first overcorrects the slogan into the claim that correlation never implies causation, which is false in general and would rule out randomised experiments, where the design rather than the association carries the warrant. The second treats controlling for confounders as a mechanical fix, when conditioning on a mediator blocks part of the causal effect and conditioning on a common effect of two variables can create a spurious association. The third takes a reversal under stratification as showing that one of the two associations must be false, when in the genuine Simpson case both are correct and the disagreement is about the population under consideration. The fourth demands a mechanism before any causal claim is acceptable, which would rule out most of epidemiology and much of economics, and which sets a standard that Hume's own analysis of constant conjunction does not require. Diagnostic question: name the intervention the claim is about, and name what is being held fixed; if no intervention can be described even in principle, the causal claim needs recasting.
depth.application: Non-blocking task with arithmetic. Construct your own Simpson's paradoxical dataset of at least eight thousand cases in two strata, choosing the two rates within each stratum and the proportions of the strata so that the pooled association reverses. Then verify by computation and report the four within-stratum rates, the two pooled rates, and the margin by which they reverse. Write four further paragraphs. First, name the confounder and explain in one sentence why it is a common cause rather than a mediator. Second, explain which comparison answers the question a policy-maker would actually be asking. Third, state what additional evidence would be needed to license a causal claim, choosing among an intervention, a natural experiment, and mechanistic evidence, and say why that route is feasible or not. Fourth, write the fallacy-avoiding version of the claim for a general audience in two sentences. Model response: with a rural stratum of ten thousand in which smoking is common and pollution low, and an urban stratum of ten thousand in which smoking is rare and pollution high, the pooled rates are fifteen per cent among smokers and twenty-five per cent among non-smokers, while the stratum rates are ten against five and thirty-five against thirty, so the reversal is ten percentage points; the confounder is residence acting through pollution, which is a common cause since it affects both smoking prevalence and cancer risk without being caused by either; the policy question concerns the effect of reducing smoking, which is answered by the stratified or intervention comparison and not by the pooled one; the additional evidence would be a cessation study or a policy-induced change in smoking, both of which approximate an intervention; the public version is that smokers in this population have lower cancer rates because smoking is concentrated in cleaner areas, and that within each area smoking is associated with higher rates. Self-review rubric, five points: (1) the arithmetic is shown and is correct; (2) both within-stratum and pooled rates are reported; (3) the confounder is correctly classified as a common cause rather than a mediator or collider; (4) the evidence route is named and its feasibility assessed; (5) the plain-language version does not overclaim beyond the design's warrant.
depth.summary: Probability raising captures part of what we mean by causation and fails in two directions, through confounders that make it insufficient and through reversals under stratification that make it unreliable as a guide to intervention. The transferable skill is to ask what intervention a causal claim is about and what is being held fixed, to distinguish common causes from mediators and colliders, and to recognise that an association can support a causal conclusion when the argument supplies the design or the mechanism that the association alone lacks. That discipline is the difference between citing a correlation and defending a causal claim, and it applies wherever arguments about policy, health, or responsibility invoke what causes what.

lessons.title: Understanding versus prediction: what an explanation adds
lessons.explanation: A model can predict accurately while leaving you with no idea why, and a philosophical argument can treat that gap as either trivial or decisive. The Stanford Encyclopedia's account of twentieth-century theories of scientific explanation shows why the two come apart. Hempel's deductive-nomological model holds that to explain a phenomenon is to derive a statement of it from premises that include at least one law, so explanation consists in subsumption under law, and the model is motivated by the idea of nomic expectability: a phenomenon is explained when it could have been expected. On that model, explanation and prediction are structurally symmetric, since the same derivation can serve either purpose, and the difference is pragmatic, depending on whether you already know the outcome. The symmetry is also the model's liability, and the entry supplies the decisive counterexamples in its section on explanatory understanding. Explanatory asymmetries show that derivability is not sufficient: the length of a flagpole's shadow can be derived from the height of the pole, the angle of the sun, and laws of rectilinear propagation, and that derivation seems explanatory, while the derivation of the pole's height from the shadow and the same laws satisfies the same criteria and does not seem explanatory at all. Something beyond derivability is doing the work, and competing accounts place it in causal structure, as in Salmon's causal-mechanical model, in statistical relevance, in unification, as in Kitcher's account, or in the pragmatic context of the question asked, as in van Fraassen's constructive empiricism. The entry on mechanisms in science supplies the vocabulary for the causal alternative: a mechanism is a structure of components and activities organised so as to produce a phenomenon, and the entry distinguishes mechanistic from purely phenomenal models, and discusses intelligibility as something a mechanistic account supplies and a black-box predictor does not.
lessons.example: Take a predictive model that scores hospital patients for risk of deterioration from their electronic records. It performs well on held-out data: the ranking of patients by score correlates with who deteriorates. Apply the accounts in turn. Under Hempel's model, a statistical prediction from a regularity is not yet an explanation at all unless the premises include a law, and a fitted model is a regularity of unknown provenance, so the model predicts without explaining, and the covering-law account would demand that the statistical relationships be lawlike. Under the causal-mechanical account, the model explains to the extent that its features are causally upstream of deterioration, and here a specific pathology appears: if the strongest feature is a measurement taken because a clinician already suspected deterioration, the model is exploiting a downstream consequence rather than a cause, and its accuracy will not survive a change in clinical practice. The practical cost is exact. A model built on such features may support triage decisions, but it cannot guide intervention, because intervening on a downstream effect of the condition does nothing to the condition. Compare the flagpole case from the entry. Both derivations satisfy the same formal criteria, and one carries causal information, which is why the shadow derivation explains and the height derivation does not. The two cases jointly show that explanatory power is not a matter of accuracy or derivability but of carrying information about the causal structure that connects the terms.
lessons.question: According to the flagpole counterexample to Hempel's model, what exactly does the shadow derivation reveal about the conditions for a successful explanation?
lessons.answer: It reveals that derivability from laws and initial conditions is not sufficient, because the derivation runs in a direction that carries no explanatory information about the phenomenon being explained
lessons.distractor: It reveals that derivability is not necessary for explanation, because the shadow can be explained without any appeal to laws of light propagation
lessons.correction: Both derivations satisfy the covering-law criteria, so the example bears on sufficiency rather than necessity, and the explanatory one does appeal to laws. The distractor locates the failure in the absence of laws, which misdescribes the case entirely, since the whole point is that the same laws are used on both sides.

depth.definitions: The deductive-nomological model holds that an explanation is a valid deductive argument whose premises include at least one law and whose conclusion states the phenomenon. Nomic expectability is the property of being derivable from laws and initial conditions, which the model identifies with being explained. The inductive-statistical model extends the pattern to statistical laws. The statistical-relevance model holds that explanation requires the partitioning of a reference class into relevant subclasses. Causal-mechanical explanation cites mechanisms and causal processes rather than regularities. Unificationist accounts hold that explanation increases by reducing the number of independent assumptions needed. Pragmatic accounts hold that what counts as an explanation depends on the question and the context. A mechanism is an organised structure of components whose activities produce a phenomenon, and a purely phenomenal model describes a regularity without representing the mechanism. Prerequisites: the causal material of lesson 98 and the analysis of explanation in lesson 71; this lesson adds the distinction between representing and predicting.
depth.mechanism: The distinction between predicting and understanding comes down to which counterfactual questions a representation can answer, and the accounts differ on which counterfactuals matter. Nomic expectability answers questions about derivation: given the laws and the initial conditions, the phenomenon was to be expected, which is why the model treats the shadow case as puzzling, since the derivation is symmetric and expectation is not. Causal accounts answer questions about manipulation: if a component were changed, what would the phenomenon do, and the flagpole case is diagnostic because the shadow does not influence the pole, so the relevant counterfactual fails in one direction and not the other. Unificationist accounts answer questions about explanatory economy: a theory that explains many phenomena with few assumptions scores better, so the advance from Kepler's regularities to Newtonian gravitation consists in subsuming planetary and terrestrial motion under one principle. Mechanistic accounts add the internal structure: components, activities, and organisation, which is what makes intelligibility possible, while the Encyclopedia also notes the limits, namely that mechanisms are defined relative to phenomena, that boundaries between them are drawn for purposes, and that purely phenomenal models can be legitimate in disciplines where mechanisms are unknown. The practical signature of the distinction is extrapolation: a representation that captures causal structure travels better to a new context than one that captures a correlation, because the correlation may be broken by the change while the mechanism persists or is modified in a predictable way.
depth.secondExample: Take Kepler's laws and Newton's theory of gravitation. Kepler's laws predict planetary positions well, and the entry's discussion of unification explains why the move to Newton is felt as an increase in understanding rather than merely an increase in accuracy: the same principle accounts for the fall of an apple, the tides, and the orbit of the moon, and that reduction in the number of independent assumptions is the explanatory gain. Notice that this gain is not a gain in predictive accuracy at the time, since Kepler's laws were already accurate for the observations then available. Contrast the readmission risk model from the first example, where prediction is strong and the causal reading is vulnerable, and a third case: a purely phenomenal model in a discipline where no mechanism is known, such as an empirical relation in a complex system. The entry's treatment suggests that such a model need not be defective, since it may be all that the state of knowledge permits, and the fault lies not in the model but in treating it as an explanation. That is the precise error to watch for: not using a predictive model, but using it as though the features it relies on were causes and as though intervening on them would change the outcome.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first infers understanding from predictive success, which is the non-sequitur this lesson exists to expose. The second demands a mechanism before any claim is acceptable, which would rule out statistical explanation and would set a standard the covering-law tradition never needed. The third identifies mechanistic explanation with reductionism, when the Encyclopedia distinguishes explanatory and ontological reductionism from the integration of fields, and offers integrative pluralism as an alternative. The fourth assumes that a law must appear in every explanation, which the causal, unificationist, and pragmatic accounts each deny in different ways. Diagnostic: ask which counterfactual questions the representation answers, whether an intervention on the highlighted variables would change the outcome, and whether the features used are upstream causes or downstream traces.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Find a predictive claim reported in a source you read this month, ideally one that uses statistics or machine learning, and produce a five-part assessment. First, state what is predicted and with what accuracy, and on what population. Second, list the features or variables on which the prediction rests, as far as the source reveals them. Third, classify each feature as plausibly upstream, plausibly downstream, or unknown relative to the outcome, and flag any that would be a consequence of the outcome rather than a cause. Fourth, state whether an intervention on the top feature would plausibly change the outcome, and if not, what the prediction can and cannot be used for. Fifth, write two sentences stating what would have to be added for the claim to count as an explanation under each of the two accounts you find most defensible. Model response for a readmission score: the claim predicts readmission risk with a stated accuracy on a defined population; the features include prior admissions, a laboratory value, and a flag indicating a follow-up appointment was scheduled; the appointment flag is plausibly downstream, since it is recorded because the patient was already judged at risk; an intervention on the flag would not reduce risk, whereas an intervention on the laboratory value might, if it is causally upstream; the model can triage but cannot guide treatment; and under the causal account an explanation would require identifying the mechanism by which the upstream features act, while under the unificationist account it would require deriving the relationship from more general principles rather than from a fitted association. Self-review rubric, five points: (1) prediction and explanation are kept separate throughout; (2) downstream features are identified with a reason; (3) the intervention question is answered rather than posed; (4) the uses the model does and does not support are stated; (5) the requirements of both named accounts are specified.
depth.summary: Explanation and prediction come apart because derivability and accuracy can hold without carrying information about what would change what. The transferable skill is to ask which counterfactuals a claim supports, to classify the features it relies on as upstream or downstream of the outcome, and to state what each account of explanation would require in addition. That habit protects against two opposite errors, the inference from predictive success to understanding, and the demand for a mechanism where a well-identified regularity is all the evidence available.

lessons.title: Capstone: reconstructing an opponent's argument in its strongest form
lessons.explanation: This capstone turns the level's tools on the act of disagreeing well. The starting point is the straw man, which the Stanford Encyclopedia treats as a variation of ignoratio elenchi, the argument that misses the point at issue. In the entry's illustration, someone who holds that industrialisation is the cause of global warming is answered by the substituted claim that all the ills besetting mankind are due to industrialisation, a claim that is easily refuted; the entry notes that two things went wrong, since the proponent does not hold the substituted claim and, even if she did, the falsity of the stronger claim would not establish the falsity of the original one. So a straw man is doubly defective, by misattribution and by non-sequitur, and the second defect is the one that survives even when the misattribution is unwitting. Evidence for the cost of this habit comes from the entry on argument and argumentation, which distinguishes adversarial from cooperative argumentation and separates the descriptive question, whether argumentation is in fact mostly adversarial, from the normative question, whether it ought to be. It records that authors who criticise overly adversarial practice include Moulton and Gilbert, and in its section on argumentative injustice it draws on the epistemic injustice literature to describe a specific failure in which a contribution is not given the credibility or engagement its content merits. Failing to reconstruct the strongest available version of an argument is one such failure when the treatment tracks the speaker's social position rather than the argument's quality. The positive method is a discipline with five moves: identify the thesis precisely, supply the premises the proponent's own commitments support, make the inference as strong as honesty permits, locate the load-bearing premise and attack there, and state what would change your mind. The principle of charity, as Davidson develops it in the theory of radical interpretation, is a constraint that makes interpretation possible at all, and it belongs here as a constraint on how you read the opponent's words rather than as a requirement to agree.
lessons.example: Work a full reconstruction and evaluation. Take the thesis that a university should stop requiring standardised admissions tests. The weak version, of the form a straw man produces, is that the university wants to admit students without any evidence of academic preparation, and refuting that version is easy and worthless. Build the strongest version from the proponent's own commitments instead. Premise one: in this institution's own admissions data, high-school grades predict degree completion at least as well as test scores, and the test adds little incremental predictive value at the margin where decisions are actually made. Premise two: where a requirement adds no predictive value and imposes a burden that falls unevenly on applicants without means, and signals a conception of merit the institution does not endorse, the institution should not require it. Premise three: the test burden falls unevenly in this applicant pool. Conclusion: the requirement should be dropped. Now evaluate properly. Premise one is empirical and contested, since the literature is mixed across institutions, disciplines, and score ranges, and the correct move is to check the claim against the relevant data rather than to assert either side. Premise two is normative and requires defence about what an admissions criterion is for, and a critic who accepts it can still argue that the test adds value in specific cases. Premise three is empirical and usually supported. Note the shape of the outcome: the strongest version of the argument is conditional on premise one holding at this institution, so the argument is not refuted by showing that tests predict well somewhere else, and it is not established by the appeal to fairness alone. Compare a case where charity has limits: consider a claim whose strongest form requires an unfalsifiable premise, such as an allegation that a hostile coalition acts in perfect secrecy and that any evidence against the allegation is part of the cover-up. The charitable reconstruction should be attempted, and its result is that the strongest version is not testable, which is a verdict about the argument rather than a licence to dismiss the speaker. Charity does not oblige you to abandon the requirement that a claim be answerable to evidence.
lessons.question: A critic shows that a proponent's stated defence of her conclusion is defective, and concludes that the conclusion is false. What is the error, and what does a fair assessment require instead?
lessons.answer: The error is treating a defective defence as a refutation of the conclusion, since a different argument may support it, and fair assessment requires reconstructing the strongest available defence before evaluating it
lessons.distractor: The error is failing to distinguish a straw man from a reductio, since the critic has refuted a stronger claim than the proponent advanced and must therefore accept the original conclusion
lessons.correction: The critic has not substituted a stronger claim, so the straw-man diagnosis does not apply here; the mistake is the inference from a bad defence to a false conclusion, which the level treats under inference rather than under distortion. The alternative error described in the distractor would also be a defect, but it is a different one and it is not what this case exhibits.

depth.definitions: Steelmanning is the practice of reconstructing an argument in the strongest form available from the proponent's own commitments, and it is contrasted with the straw man, a variation of ignoratio elenchi in which the position is substituted so as to be easier to refute. The fallacy fallacy is the inference from the defectiveness of an argument to the falsehood of its conclusion. The principle of charity, in Davidson's use, is a constraint on interpretation requiring that a speaker be interpreted so as to be largely right about the world, because interpretation is only possible on that assumption; it operationalises as a constraint on reading rather than as a demand for agreement. Adversarial and cooperative argumentation name two ways of conducting a dispute, and the entry separates the descriptive question of which predominates from the normative question of which ought to. Argumentative injustice is a failure of engagement or credibility attribution that tracks irrelevant social features rather than the merits. Prerequisites: the validity and soundness material of lesson 91, the fallacy material of lesson 92, and the epistemic injustice material of lesson 87.
depth.mechanism: The reason charity is not merely good manners is that an argument is a set of propositions and inferences, so a criticism aimed at propositions the proponent does not hold carries no information about her position. Every unit of epistemic value a criticism can have comes from the fidelity of the reconstruction, which means that the reconstruction, not the rebuttal, is where the work is. The corollary is that a criticism which only succeeds against a weakened version is evidence that the critic has not located the real difficulty, which is diagnostic information about the criticism rather than about the target. The second mechanism is dialectical. In an adversarial frame, the aim is to win, and misattribution is an efficient way to win, so the frame systematically produces it. The argumentation literature's contrast between adversarial and cooperative framing is about this incentive structure rather than about politeness, and the literature on argumentative injustice adds that the resulting failures of engagement are unevenly distributed, falling on speakers whose social position already disposes an audience to discount them. Two limits belong with the method. First, the strongest version must be a version of what the proponent actually holds, and an upgrading reconstruction must be flagged as a reconstruction and offered in her terms, since otherwise charity becomes substitution from the other direction. Second, when the strongest available version is unfalsifiable, the honest verdict is that the argument cannot bear the weight placed on it, and charitable reconstruction does not require treating unfalsifiability as strength.
depth.secondExample: Use the method where it helps the critic rather than the target. Suppose two parties disagree about a housing policy and appear to be talking past each other. Party one argues that the policy will fail because construction costs will not fall; party two argues that the policy is unjust because it displaces existing tenants. Reconstructed charitably, these are not competing predictions but answers to different questions, one empirical about feasibility and one normative about distribution, and the appearance of contradiction comes from each side treating its premise as decisive. Making the premises explicit reveals that party one's claim rests on an estimate that can be checked and that party two's claim rests on a moral premise that is not settled by the estimate, so the disagreement has two parts that require different treatment. The critic's gain is that the empirical dispute can now be resolved, or shown to be resolvable, without either side surrendering its normative position, which is a better outcome than the exchange of misattributions that the adversarial frame produces. Contrast that with a case where the reconstruction reveals an incompatibility that no reframing removes, such as two incompatible principles about what may be done to a person without consent, where the honest verdict is that a genuine normative disagreement remains. The method is not a device for manufacturing agreement; it is a device for identifying where the disagreement actually lies.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first treats charity as agreement, which confuses a constraint on interpretation with a concession. The second reconstructs the strongest possible version rather than the strongest version the proponent actually holds, which produces the mirror image of a straw man, a criticism the proponent can correctly disown. The third commits the fallacy fallacy, rejecting a conclusion because one defence of it failed. The fourth assumes the proponent must accept your reconstruction, when the point of offering it is to invite correction, and a proponent who disowns it owes you her own version, which is itself progress. Diagnostic: before writing a criticism, state the target's thesis in one sentence and check whether the proponent would sign it; then state which premise you intend to attack and why attacking that premise bears on the conclusion rather than on a neighbouring claim.
depth.application: Non-blocking capstone task. Choose one position you reject on a matter you care about. Write a reconstruction with five numbered components. First, the thesis in one sentence, in terms its proponent would accept. Second, premises at least three, drawn from the proponent's own commitments and labelled empirical or normative. Third, the inference, rendered so that it is valid or as close to valid as honesty permits. Fourth, the weakest link, named as a premise or an inference, with the specific evidence or argument that would damage it and what would instead strengthen it. Fifth, your verdict, distinguishing three possibilities: the premise is false, the inference fails, or the conclusion may be true but this argument does not establish it. Finish with one paragraph stating what would change your own mind about the matter. Model response for a position you reject about criminal sentencing: the thesis is that sentences should be set by guidelines rather than judicial discretion; the empirical premise is that guidelines reduce unexplained variation in similar cases; the normative premise is that like cases must be treated alike and that unexplained variation is a form of unfairness; the inference is that if guidelines reduce variation and variation is unfair, guidelines are required; the weakest link is the empirical premise, since guidelines can shift variation to charging decisions rather than remove it, and the evidence that would damage it is a study showing displacement to other stages; the verdict is that the conclusion may be defensible but this argument does not establish it, because the fairness premise requires an account of which variations are unjustified, and the last paragraph states that evidence of systematic bias within guideline ranges would move you toward a different remedy. Self-review rubric, five points: (1) the thesis would be signed by its proponent; (2) every premise is labelled and sourced from the proponent's commitments; (3) the inference is rendered rather than paraphrased; (4) the verdict distinguishes the three failure types; (5) the paragraph on what would change your mind is specific enough to be falsified by a future event.
depth.summary: Disagreeing well is a technical skill with identifiable failure modes, and the straw man is only the most visible of them: misattribution, the fallacy fallacy, and the upgrading of a position beyond what its proponent holds are the others. The transferable method is to reconstruct the thesis, supply the premises the proponent's own commitments support, render the inference, attack the load-bearing premise, and state what would change your mind. Applied across the level, that method is what converts the vocabulary of validity, fallacies, testimony, vagueness, causation, and explanation into a practice, since each of those tools is a way of locating precisely what an argument needs and where it fails.
